title: Anti-AI sentiment doesn't matter much – three years of experience
author: playthelastsecret
selftext:
It's been more than three years that we started making games (visual novels) using AI art and published them on Steam. (We were indeed one of the first.) Since then, we have been asked again and again how difficult this is, given the overall strong anti-AI sentiment.

**The answer:** Forget it!

We have a few bad reviews because of that, but our first AI generated game still got 88% positive reviews in Steam, and our best one has 93%. And download numbers are by no means lower than for our non-AI visual novel. – Okay, we are small, so no review bombing and brigading happened to us, like it would if we were AAA, but still, the whole thing teaches one important lesson:

**Players in general do not care whether it's AI made or not!**

They want to play a good game. Not AI *slop*, not an asset flip, not shuffle ware. Just a good game. And they don't care how it's made, as long as it is good!

If in opinion polls most people say they dislike generative AI... well, most people say what they think they are supposed to say... And then they still use ChatGPT, and they still play our games.

**So, don't worry too much about this whole controversy. It's definitely overvalued.**

replies.author: CircularSeasoning
replies.body:
Not arguing here, just musing, hope you don't mind...

AI *is*, in many senses, human-made. It's a tool made by humans, trained on humans, and directed by humans.

I think a better way to say it is "trying to pass AI as hand-made". That at least avoids the half-true idea that AI has nothing to do with humanity, or human-ness. The prime mover behind every AI is a human. Even the agent AIs. Some human had to have the smarts and intent to get it going, when you trace it back to origin.

Another thought. You dig a hole with your hands or you dig it with a spade, or an excavator? It's still what we call "a human-made hole" as opposed to some random happenstance of nature.

Artificial intelligence means:

Intelligence that is artificial.

What is artificial? Artificial means, "made by man, not nature". 

So something made with use of AI is more like hyper-human. More human than even a human. Interestingly, that's one of the reasons people can be put off by it. Because it exhibits or amplifies the human tendency to shape, control, and perfect nature to our will so strongly that we often forget that nature and 'real life' is, after all, full of imperfections.

In a funny way, this logic may lead one to begin to embrace things that exihibit AI sloppiness as showing something that is actually very inherently human.

Think about it. We have conquered the use of advanced math to write poems, essays, and apps... and yet so many people are using this powerful AI technology in such lazy (unrefined) ways. Oh look, it makes 90% of an epic image! <stops there and publishes it as-is>. Lol. Silly, human-like humans. So much potential, so wasted on being 10% less than what we could be if only we believed in ourselves or worked just 10% more.

And then there's actual spam and automated content generation by someone who is totally uninvolved and disinterested in the final products. Yeah, yeah, that sucks. No one who is pro-AI argues about that stuff.

comments.author: ponderdiggums
comments.body:
Anti-AI sentiment is born from a prevelance of slop. Don't make slop, and people will probably be more open to trying your game. 

You can avoid making slop with lots of QA, playtesting and a ton of iteration. Put care and effort into it in a way that makes the players feel like you care about your own product. Make assets or pay someone to make them, if you're using AI art clean it up and animate those assets (though it's really not that hard to make pixel art, aesprite is super easy to learn). Don't just generate audio, mix it properly. 

I know a lot of AI bros will reel at the notion of producing a labor of love, but that reluctance to approach games as an artform is why folks will be prone to view said output as slop.

replies.author: playthelastsecret
replies.body:
Thank you. Well, "My Silly Science Summer" is not as successful, to be honest. I think without a romance hook, it is difficult to interest too many girls either... but the romance just didn't fit: We didn't want handsome and smart boys explaining science to the female protagonist. That would have been the very wrong message...

We use translation AI (DeepL) for all our games. Of course, manual proofreading is needed afterwards.

For "Sweet Science" and TBI we used AI art. For "My Silly Science Summer", DQ and KM we also used AI music. For DQ we also let the AI write some of the stories (with heavy editing afterwards). That was an experiment, and we learned that the best way is to do a mixed approach: Plan and outline the story by hand in all small details. Then instruct the AI (Claude) to write a first draft of a scene. Then improve that. Then edit it manually (quite heavily). We use this method now in new productions like KM, and I think the quality is optimal that way. Writing is also a bit faster than purely manual, but the big difference is quality. 

Finally, we use AI now for help with coding minigames. I'm not revealing anything new with that, but this speeds up coding times a lot.
